Seller’s prep list
Sold · What happens next

Everything between sold and keys

40 things, in the order they need doing, counted back from your closing date. The ones that cost real money if they are missed are marked.

Start here

Three things go wrong more than everything else combined

01

Keep the house insured until your lawyer says it closed

Not until closing day. Until your lawyer confirms the deal registered and the money moved. Closings slip by a day fairly often, and a house that burns while it is uninsured and still in your name is your loss.

02

Ask your lender for the payout figure the day the deal is firm

Breaking a mortgage early carries a charge, and on a fixed rate it is usually the biggest single cost of selling. You want that number in writing early, while you can still do something about it.

03

Book the movers before you do anything else on this page

Most Ontario deals close on the last business day of the month, so every seller in the province wants the same truck on the same morning. In a condo the elevator books out too.

Add your closing date.

As soon as the sale is firm

Start now

Five calls in the first week. Everything after this is easier if these five happen now.

  • Send the signed agreement to your lawyer

    If you do not have a real estate lawyer yet, get one this week. Your lawyer needs the full agreement including every amendment and waiver, not just the front page. They handle the transfer of title, the payout of your mortgage and the money, and they cannot start until they have the paperwork.

  • Tell your lender you are selling, and ask for the payout statement
    Costs money

    Ask for three things in writing: the balance, the discharge fee, and the prepayment charge for ending the term early. On a fixed rate that charge is worked out one of two ways and one of them is far larger, so get the actual figure rather than a rule of thumb. If you are buying again, ask in the same call whether your mortgage can move to the new home at the same rate, and how many days the lender allows between the two closings.

  • Book the movers

    Get the quote in writing with the date, the start time, the two addresses, the price, and what their insurance covers if something of yours breaks. Month end fills first because most closings land there.

  • Ask property management for the moving rules and book the elevator
    Condo

    Buildings set the hours, the entrance, and the notice they need, which runs from about a week to a month. Most also want a deposit you get back if nothing is damaged, and a certificate of insurance from your mover naming the building. Ask the mover for that certificate when you book, not on the morning, because a rejection at eight o'clock costs you the elevator slot.

  • Tell your insurer the closing date, and do not cancel anything
    Do not skip

    You are responsible for the house until it legally changes hands. Give your insurer the date so the policy runs past it, and leave the cancelling until your lawyer confirms the deal is done.

  • Reread what you agreed to leave behind

    Anything bolted, wired or plumbed in is a fixture and stays unless the agreement says in writing that you are taking it. Anything loose is a chattel and goes with you unless the agreement says in writing that it stays. The light fixture you meant to keep, the shed, the mounted television, the appliances: check each one now, while there is still time to talk about it, rather than on closing morning when it becomes a dispute.

About two months out

60 days before closing

The paperwork that takes other people time. Start it before you start packing.

  • Find every rental contract and decide: pay it out, or hand it over
    Costs moneyRented equipment

    Water heater, furnace, air conditioner, water softener, air exchanger, alarm gear. These companies usually register a notice against your title, so your lawyer has to deal with it either way. Either the buyer agrees to take the contract over, which needs to be in the agreement, or you pay it out before closing. Ask each company for the buyout figure now: it drops as the equipment ages and it is not a number you want to discover on closing day.

  • Send your lawyer the rest of what they asked for

    Usually: photo identification for everyone on title, your mortgage details, any rental contracts, the survey if you have one, and your forwarding address. If anyone on title has changed their name, married, separated or died since you bought, tell them now, because that adds steps.

  • Get the status certificate ordered if the buyer has not
    Condo

    The buyer's side usually orders it, but it comes from your corporation and it carries the moving rules you will need anyway. Ask management how long they take.

  • Book anything you agreed to fix

    If the deal included repairs, get them done and keep the invoices. The buyer walks through before closing and will look for exactly these.

  • Line your two closing dates up with your lawyer
    If buying too

    Selling and buying on the same day is normal and it is tight: the money from your sale usually funds your purchase, and it moves in the afternoon. If the dates do not line up you need bridge financing arranged in advance, not on the day.

  • Start giving things away

    Movers charge by weight or by hour. Everything you do not take is money you do not spend, and this is the part that always takes longer than people expect.

One month out

30 days before closing

Address changes and utilities. Mail forwarding takes a week and a half to switch on, so it starts here.

  • Set up mail forwarding

    Canada Post takes five to ten business days to start, so buying it now means it is live on the day you leave. You can forward for one person or for everyone at the address, and you can extend it later. Treat it as a safety net rather than the plan: it catches what you forget to change.

    Set up forwarding at Canada Post
  • Update your driver's licence, plates and health card
    Do not skip

    Ontario law gives you six days after you move to update your driver's licence and vehicle permit. One online session covers the licence, the plates, the health card and the photo card together.

    Change your address with ServiceOntario
  • Book the final readings for the day of closing, not before
    Do not skip

    Electricity, gas, water, internet, telephone. Give each one the closing date as the last day in your name. Do not shut anything off early: the buyer walks through before closing and needs the lights and the furnace to work. Your electricity company depends on where you live rather than who you buy from, so check the bill for the name if you are not sure.

    Find your local hydro utility
  • Cancel or move the services that come to the house

    Alarm monitoring, lawn care, snow clearing, pool service, pest control, cleaners, water delivery, propane. Some will move with you and some will not, and most want notice.

  • Work through the address list

    Bank and credit cards, employer and payroll, the Canada Revenue Agency, your pension and investment accounts, car and life insurance, the schools, your doctor, dentist, pharmacy and veterinarian, any subscription that arrives in a box, and the gym. The tax one matters more than it looks: a refund or a benefit cheque sent to an old address is slow to untangle.

    • Bank, credit cards, loans
    • Employer and payroll
    • Canada Revenue Agency
    • Pension and investments
    • Car and life insurance
    • Schools and daycare
    • Doctor, dentist, pharmacy
    • Veterinarian
    • Subscriptions and deliveries
    • Gym and memberships
  • Ask for your records if you are leaving the area

    Medical, dental and veterinary files, and the children's school records. Easier to request while you are still a current patient.

  • Start eating the freezer

    Frozen and tinned food is heavy, and most movers will not take anything that can leak or thaw.

Two weeks out

14 days before closing

Confirm what you booked, and start gathering what the buyer needs on the other side.

  • Confirm the movers in writing

    Date, arrival time, both addresses, the price and what happens if the closing moves by a day. Ask what they will not carry: paint, propane, cleaning chemicals and anything that burns are usually refused.

  • Confirm the elevator and get the insurance certificate to management
    Condo

    Call the office rather than assuming the booking held. Send the mover's certificate of insurance now so someone has time to read it.

  • Gather every key, remote and code in the house

    Front, back, side, garage, shed, gate, mailbox, storage locker, window locks, the pool gate. Garage remotes and the keypad code. The alarm code and the monitoring company's password. Anything you hold that the buyer will need, including the copies at your neighbour's and your mother's.

  • Arrange somewhere for the children and the pets to be

    Moving day is doors propped open, strangers carrying heavy things, and nobody watching the driveway.

  • Pack the first night box and keep it with you

    Bedding, towels, toilet paper, soap, phone chargers, medication, coffee and something to make it in, a change of clothes, basic tools, and the paperwork for the closing. This box travels in your car, never in the truck.

The last week

7 days before closing

Signing, and the last of the loose ends.

  • Sign at your lawyer's office

    This is usually a few days before closing rather than on the day. Bring photo identification for everyone on title. Confirm at the same time exactly where your money goes and how it gets there.

  • Return the equipment that belongs to somebody else

    Cable boxes, modems, alarm panels, propane tanks, water cooler bottles, library books. Anything you keep gets billed to you months later at a price nobody would agree to in advance.

  • Sort out where the truck parks

    On a narrow street or downtown you may need a permit from the city, and it takes a few days. In a condo the loading dock is booked with the elevator.

  • Top up the oil or propane if the agreement says so
    House

    Fuel in a tank is usually settled between the two sides at closing. Get the fill done and give your lawyer the receipt.

Moving day

1 day before closing

The house has to be empty, clean, and holding everything you agreed to leave.

  • Photograph every meter
    Do not skip

    Electricity, gas, water. Get the numbers legible and the date on the photo. This is the whole of your defence against a final bill that covers somebody else's use.

  • Walk the house yourself, opening everything

    Every cupboard and closet, the medicine cabinet, behind the washer and dryer, the dishwasher, the oven drawer, the crawl space, the attic hatch, the garage rafters, the shed, under the deck, the side of the house. This is where things get left.

  • Leave it broom clean

    Floors swept, carpets vacuumed, surfaces wiped, nothing left behind. Nothing at the curb either: what you leave for the garbage becomes the buyer's problem and, quite often, your bill. If the agreement asks for more than broom clean, do what it says.

  • Leave a pack on the kitchen counter

    This is the part sellers are remembered for. Appliance manuals and warranties, the alarm code and the monitoring company, the leftover paint labelled by room, the extra tiles and flooring, the pool or spa instructions, the garbage and recycling days, the septic or well paperwork, and the trades you would call again. It costs you nothing and it is the difference between a house and a handover.

    • Manuals and warranties
    • Alarm code and monitoring company
    • Leftover paint, labelled by room
    • Spare tiles and flooring
    • Pool, spa, septic or well notes
    • Garbage and recycling days
    • Trades worth calling again
  • Photograph the empty house

    Every room, the garage, the yard. Five minutes now, and any argument about the condition you left it in is over before it starts.

Closing day

Closing day

Short list. Mostly it is your lawyer's day.

  • Get every key to your lawyer

    Usually first thing in the morning unless they told you otherwise. Label them. The buyer does not get in until the money and the title have both moved, and your keys are what is waiting.

  • Stay reachable

    Deals close on the day but rarely at a set hour, and if something needs a signature it needs it quickly.

  • Still do not cancel your insurance
    Do not skip

    Wait for your lawyer to confirm the transfer registered and the money was released. That confirmation is the moment the house stops being your risk.

The week after

7 days after closing

Three things, then it is finished.

  • Now cancel the insurance

    Once your lawyer has confirmed it closed. Ask for the refund of whatever you prepaid.

  • Watch for the final bills

    Utility accounts close on a reading rather than on your instruction, so the last bill arrives a few weeks later and goes to the forwarded address. Check it against the meter photos you took.

  • Keep the closing package somewhere you will find it

    The statement of adjustments and the lawyer's reporting letter are tax documents. Keep them with the paperwork from when you bought.

  • Report the sale on next year's tax return
    Do not skip

    Every home sale gets reported, including one that is fully covered by the principal residence exemption. Not reporting it can cost one hundred dollars a month up to eight thousand. Your accountant needs the date you bought, the date you sold, and both prices.

    Reporting the sale of your principal residence



This is a general list, not advice about your deal. Your agreement of purchase and sale, your lawyer and your lender decide what actually applies to you, and where any of them says something different from this page, they are right and this page is wrong. It is written for Ontario. Ask THE AGENCY about anything here that does not look like your situation.
